title: Recurrent pregnancy loss guidelines: Earlier evaluation
summary: Updated recurrent pregnancy loss guidelines support evaluation after two losses, including biochemical pregnancies. Learn about guideline-aligned testing.
body_markdown:
Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) remains one of the most challenging experiences in reproductive care. Each pregnancy loss carries significant emotional implications for patients and families, making timely assessment and communication especially important. Women’s health providers and primary care clinicians alike play an important role in identifying patients who meet updated criteria for RPL and facilitating timely referral, testing, and reproductive evaluation.


## New recurrent pregnancy loss guidelines


The[American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) now defines recurrent pregnancy loss](https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/recurrent-pregnancy-loss-a-committee-opinion-2026/) as two or more pregnancy losses, rather than three, and recognizes pregnancies confirmed by urine or blood hCG, including biochemical pregnancies, as part of the definition. The change reflects evidence that recurrence risk may be apparent after two losses, and that biochemical pregnancy losses affect future pregnancy risk similarly to clinically recognized losses. ASRM also notes that requiring ultrasound or tissue confirmation may exclude some early losses because access to early pregnancy care is variable across patient populations. This updated definition aligns with[ACOG guidance](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/repeated-miscarriages) recommending evaluation after two miscarriages and supports earlier identification of patients who may benefit from further assessment.


This change represents a meaningful shift in clinical practice.


## The case for earlier recurrent pregnancy loss evaluation


Pregnancy loss is common, and many first-trimester miscarriages occur because of sporadic chromosomal abnormalities. However, patients experiencing recurrent loss may have underlying genetic, anatomic, endocrine, immunologic, or other contributing factors that warrant investigation.


Earlier evaluation supports:


- More timely identification of potential causes
- Improved counseling and care continuity
- Reduced uncertainty for patients and families
- Alignment with current ASRM and ACOG pregnancy loss guidelines


It is important to note that[more than half of patients with repeated miscarriages may not have an identifiable cause](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/repeated-miscarriages) , even after evaluation.


Even when a definitive cause is not identified, establishing a clear diagnostic pathway can provide reassurance and support informed next steps.[ASRM notes that many patients with RPL](https://www.asrm.org/practice-guidance/practice-committee-documents/recurrent-pregnancy-loss-a-committee-opinion-2026/) may ultimately achieve a successful pregnancy, even when a specific cause is not found.


The evolution of RPL recommendations reflects a broader shift toward earlier risk identification and intervention, rather than waiting for a third loss before initiating diagnostic workup, which may reduce delays in care and help patients make more informed reproductive decisions.


## Recommended recurrent pregnancy loss testing


ASRM does not designate a single standardized recurrent pregnancy loss panel. Instead, the guidance recommends a structured evaluation based on patient history, clinical presentation, and suspected underlying causes.


Recommended assessments may include:


- **Genetic evaluation of miscarriage tissue** to identify chromosomal changes. Microarray is preferred over chromosome analysis due to its technical advantages.
- **Uterine cavity evaluation** (e.g., HSG, saline infusion sonography, or hysteroscopy) to assess anatomic factors associated with pregnancy loss
- **Targeted laboratory testing** , including antiphospholipid antibody testing, thyroid assessment, hemoglobin A1c, or prolactin testing when clinically indicated
- **Additional evaluations of select patients,** such as parental karyotyping, chronic endometritis assessment, or sperm DNA fragmentation testing


Providers should consult the latest ASRM guidelines when determining the most appropriate evaluation strategy for each patient.


## Earlier recurrent pregnancy loss evaluation, clearer answers, and more personalized care


The recent update to the recurrent pregnancy loss guidelines shift evaluation earlier in the patient journey and expands the population eligible for assessment.


A streamlined testing strategy can help reduce delays, support diagnostic clarity, and improve the patient experience during a highly sensitive time. Earlier evaluation may help providers identify potential causes sooner and deliver more personalized reproductive care.
